title: GPU and inference basics
summary: How a GPU runs a model, when work is math- or memory-bound, why decode is bandwidth-bound, how quantization, the KV cache, batching and multiple GPUs change that, and how to measure it.
outcomes: Explain how SMs, warps, HBM and on-chip memory work together and why GPUs need many threads in flight
Compute arithmetic intensity, including the T/2 reuse of a tile, and classify an operation as math-bound or memory-bound
Estimate prefill time, the attention share at long context, and the decode floor (weight bytes / bandwidth)
Compute weight bytes and the decode floor for FP16, INT8 and INT4, and explain why weight-only quantization helps decode, not prefill
Compute KV-cache size per token and how many sequences fit in GPU memory
Explain how batching and continuous batching trade per-user latency for throughput, and why a joining prefill stalls decode
Estimate per-GPU memory and decode time under tensor parallelism, and explain why more GPUs give diminishing latency gains
Time prefill and decode correctly and compute MBU to compare a measurement with the bandwidth floor

lessons.title: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory

blocks.md:
Your GPT from scratch runs the same forward pass on a laptop CPU and on a data-center GPU, yet the GPU is far faster. To reason about inference cost you need a mental model of *why*, and of where the GPU still gets stuck.

We will use one concrete chip throughout: the **NVIDIA A100 80GB (SXM)**, whose numbers are published in NVIDIA's datasheet and performance guides. SXM is NVIDIA's socketed module form factor for servers, as opposed to the PCIe plug-in card. The variant matters for our numbers: the 80GB PCIe card reads memory at 1,935 GB/s, the SXM one at 2,039 GB/s.

NVIDIA's performance guide describes a GPU as three parts:

- **Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs)**: the compute units. An A100 has 108 of them. Each SM has its own instruction schedulers, a register file, and on-chip memory.
- **L2 cache**: 40 MB shared by all SMs.
- **HBM** (high-bandwidth memory): the GPU's main memory, DRAM chips stacked in towers beside the GPU chip and wired to it by a bus thousands of bits wide, which is where its bandwidth comes from. 80 GB on this card, readable at up to 2,039 GB/s.

The model weights live in HBM. Every time a layer runs, its weights must travel from HBM, through L2, into an SM before any math happens.

blocks.title: Where data lives on an A100 and how it reaches the math units

scenes.caption: At startup the weights are copied once from host memory into HBM. After that, inference never needs the CPU for the math.
Each layer's weights stream from HBM through the shared L2 cache. This path tops out at about 2 TB/s on this card.
Work is split across 108 SMs. Each one runs many threads at once, so the chip needs lots of independent work to stay busy.

Inside an SM, tiles sit in registers (256 KB per SM) and shared memory, an on-chip scratchpad (up to 164 KB per SM) that the program fills itself, next to the Tensor Cores: units that do a small matrix multiply-add per instruction.
The key imbalance: the Tensor Cores can do 312 trillion FP16 operations per second, but HBM delivers only about 2 trillion bytes per second.

blocks.md:
Where do those two numbers come from? Peak math is SMs x clock rate x work per clock. Each A100 SM's Tensor Cores finish 1,024 FP16 multiply-adds per clock cycle, and a multiply-add counts as 2 floating-point operations (FLOPs). So 108 SMs x 1.41 GHz x 1,024 x 2 is about $312\times10^{12}$ FLOP/s. The datasheet also lists 624, but only for a special sparse mode where half the weights are zero; this course uses the dense 312.

The 2,039 GB/s is the HBM bandwidth from the datasheet. Divide one by the other: in the time HBM delivers one byte, the Tensor Cores could do about 153 operations. The next lesson builds on that ratio.

Software sees the chip through CUDA, NVIDIA's platform for writing general GPU programs (the name began as Compute Unified Device Architecture), and its thread hierarchy. A **kernel** (a function launched on the GPU) runs as a **grid**: the full set of **thread blocks** launched for it. A thread block is a group of up to 1,024 threads; each block is placed on one SM, and its threads can share that SM's shared memory. Inside a block, threads are grouped into **warps** of 32 that execute the same instruction together (NVIDIA calls this SIMT, single instruction multiple threads).

An A100 SM can hold up to 64 warps at once. That number matters because of how the GPU copes with slow memory.

blocks.title: Hiding memory latency by switching between warps

scenes.caption: Simplified, illustrative timing: one warp alone does 1 unit of math, waits 4 units for HBM, then does 1 more unit. Run warps strictly one after another and 4 warps take 24 units.

The scheduler instead issues math from whichever warp is ready. Toy rule: one warp does math per unit, loads overlap freely, and a warp's second math starts when its load returns. Warp 3's load returns at 8, so all finish at 9.

blocks.md: A GPU is a throughput machine. It hides slow memory by keeping many warps in flight, not by making any single access fast. Give it too little parallel work and the SMs sit idle.

More cores does not mean every program runs faster. If each operation reads a lot of data and does little math per byte, the SMs wait on HBM no matter how many there are. The next lesson turns this into a number.

blocks.question: A kernel is launched with only 20 thread blocks on an A100 (108 SMs), one block per SM at a time. What is the most likely problem?
options: HBM capacity is exceeded
Most SMs have no work, so the GPU is underused regardless of memory speed
The warps are too large, so threads diverge
The L2 cache is too small to hold 20 blocks
blocks.explain: Each thread block runs on one SM, so 20 blocks occupy at most 20 of 108 SMs. NVIDIA's guide recommends launching several times more blocks than SMs. This is a latency or parallelism limit, not a memory capacity issue.

blocks.question: Why does the GPU keep many warps resident on each SM?
options: So that while some warps wait for memory, others can execute math
Because each warp can only run one instruction in its lifetime
To increase the size of HBM
Because warps of 32 threads cannot share an SM
blocks.explain: GPUs hide dependent instruction and memory latency by switching to other ready warps. That is why the number of threads needed is much larger than the number of execution units.

lessons.title: Math-bound or memory-bound: arithmetic intensity and the roofline

blocks.md: Any GPU operation spends time on two things: moving bytes between HBM and the SMs, and doing arithmetic. NVIDIA's guide uses a simple model where these overlap, so the slower one decides the run time.

blocks.caption: Simplified: real kernels also spend time on address math, launches and imperfect overlap.

blocks.md: Write the comparison out: $T_{\text{math}} > T_{\text{mem}}$ means FLOPs divided by peak FLOP/s is more than bytes divided by bandwidth. Multiply both sides by peak FLOP/s and divide both by bytes, and you get FLOPs per byte on the left and peak FLOP/s per unit of bandwidth on the right: a comparison of two ratios. **Arithmetic intensity** is FLOPs per byte moved, a property of the operation. The **ops:byte ratio** is peak FLOP/s divided by bandwidth, a property of the chip. It is also called the ridge point, because on the roofline plot below it is where the sloped part of the roof meets the flat part.

blocks.caption: On an A100 an operation must do about 153 FLOPs per byte of HBM traffic to keep the Tensor Cores busy.

blocks.md:
Start tiny. **ReLU** (rectified linear unit), which outputs max(x, 0), on FP16 data reads 2 bytes and writes 2 bytes per element and does 1 operation: intensity $1/4 = 0.25$ FLOP/B. It is hopelessly memory-bound.

A **general matrix multiply** (GEMM) of an $M\times K$ matrix by a $K\times N$ matrix does $2MNK$ FLOPs: the output has $M\times N$ entries, each a dot product of length $K$, which costs $K$ multiplies and $K$ adds. With FP16 (2 bytes per number) it moves $2(MK + KN + MN)$ bytes if each matrix is touched once: read both inputs, write the output.

blocks.caption: Divide the two: 2MNK floating-point operations over 2 times (MK plus KN plus MN) bytes. The twos cancel, leaving MNK over (MK plus KN plus MN).

blocks.prompt: A linear layer with 1024 inputs and 4096 outputs is applied to a batch of 1 vector (M = 1). Guess its arithmetic intensity, then compare it with the A100 ridge of 153.
blocks.reveal: Plug in $M=1, K=1024, N=4096$: the top is $MNK = 4{,}194{,}304$ and the bottom is $1{,}024 + 4{,}194{,}304 + 4{,}096 = 4{,}199{,}424$, so about **1.00 FLOP/B**. A matrix-vector product reads every weight once and uses it for one multiply-add, so intensity can never exceed about 1. At batch 512 the same layer reaches **315 FLOP/B**, because each weight byte is reused 512 times.

blocks.md: Now turn the time model into a speed. The FLOP/s an operation attains is its FLOPs divided by $T$. Dividing FLOPs by each term of the max gives peak FLOP/s for the math term and bandwidth x intensity for the memory term, and the slower term wins, so the smaller of the two is what you get. Plot that against intensity on log axes and it looks like a roof: a slope that rises with intensity, then a flat ceiling at peak. That picture is the **roofline model** (Williams, Waterman and Patterson, 2009).

blocks.caption: The roofline: the slope is bandwidth times intensity, the flat part is peak math, and they meet at intensity = peak over bandwidth, the ridge.

blocks.title: The A100 roofline: attainable FLOP/s vs arithmetic intensity

scenes.caption: Left of the ridge, the sloped roof is bandwidth x intensity: memory-bound. Right of it, the flat roof is peak math: math-bound. A100 ridge is about 153 FLOP/B.
A batch-1 linear layer (intensity about 1) can reach at most about 2 TFLOP/s, roughly 0.7% of the Tensor Cores. That is the regime of generating one token for one user.

The ridge moved right from V100 (125 TFLOP/s over 900 GB/s, about 139) to A100 (about 153). Here is a hypothetical chip with peak 1000 and 3.35 TB/s: low-intensity work gains only from the extra bandwidth.
Back on the A100: an 8192-sided square GEMM (intensity 8192/3, about 2,731) sits on the flat roof. Training-style big batches live here.

blocks.md: The NVIDIA guide's own example: an 8192 x 128 x 8192 GEMM has intensity 124.1 FLOP/B. That was memory-bound on a V100 (ridge about 139) and is still below the A100 ridge of 153.
Compare arithmetic intensity with the chip's ops:byte ratio. Below it, speed is set by bytes moved, and adding FLOPs is nearly free. Above it, speed is set by FLOPs.

Intensity counts HBM traffic, not every load. Good kernels tile data into shared memory and registers so each HBM byte is reused many times; a naive kernel that re-reads HBM has a much lower effective intensity than the formula suggests.

Why does tiling raise intensity? Take one output tile of $T\times T$ values of $C = AB$, with inner dimension $K$. To compute it, an SM loads a $T\times K$ strip of rows of $A$ and a $K\times T$ strip of columns of $B$: $2TK$ values, or $4TK$ bytes in FP16. It then does $2T^2K$ FLOPs on them, because each of the $T^2$ outputs is a dot product of length $K$. Divide the two and $K$ cancels.

blocks.caption: Counted against the memory that feeds the tile (shared memory and registers loading from L2 or HBM). Each loaded value is reused T times.

blocks.title: One output tile of C and the strips of A and B it reads

scenes.caption: T = 1: one output of C needs one row of A and one column of B, 2K values for 2K FLOPs. That is 0.5 FLOP/B, as bad as a matrix-vector product.
T = 2: four outputs share 2 rows of A and 2 columns of B. Twice the data, four times the FLOPs: 1 FLOP/B.
T = 4: sixteen outputs from 4 rows and 4 columns, 2 FLOP/B. Every value brought on chip is used T times before it is dropped.
Real tiles are larger: T = 16 gives 8 FLOP/B and T = 128 gives 64 FLOP/B. Bigger tiles need more registers and shared memory, which caps T.

blocks.md:
Notice that even $T = 128$ gives 64 FLOP/B, below the A100 ridge of 153. Shared-memory tiling alone does not make a big GEMM math-bound. The rest of the reuse comes from the 40 MB L2 cache: many thread blocks run at the same time and read the same strips of $A$ and $B$, so HBM serves far fewer bytes than the sum of every tile's loads. Reuse is a hierarchy: registers, shared memory, then L2.

This course only needs the counting. The *GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing* course builds a shared-memory tiled kernel (a transpose), and the *Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement* course draws one roof per memory level.

blocks.question: Elementwise operations (add, ReLU, LayerNorm) are at most a few FLOP/B. What is the standard way to make them cheaper on a GPU?
options: Use more Tensor Cores
Fuse them into the neighbouring kernel so the data is not written to and re-read from HBM
Increase the clock speed
Split them across more thread blocks
blocks.explain: They are memory-bound, so the only lever is fewer bytes moved. Fusing several elementwise steps into one kernel keeps the intermediate values on chip. More math units do not help a memory-bound operation.

blocks.question: A GPU has peak 1,000 TFLOP/s and 4 TB/s of bandwidth. An operation has intensity 100 FLOP/B. Which is it?
options: Math-bound, since 100 is a large intensity
Memory-bound, attaining at most 100 TFLOP/s
Memory-bound, attaining at most 400 TFLOP/s
Exactly at the ridge
blocks.explain: Ridge = 1000 / 4 = 250 FLOP/B. 100 is below it, so the roof is 4 TB/s x 100 FLOP/B = 400 TFLOP/s.

blocks.question: A kernel author shrinks the output tile from 128 x 128 to 64 x 64, keeping K the same. What happens to each tile's arithmetic intensity?
options: Nothing changes: intensity depends only on M, N and K
It doubles, because smaller tiles fit better in shared memory
The total FLOPs of the GEMM halve
It halves, from 64 to 32 FLOP/B against the memory feeding the tile
blocks.explain: Intensity of a tile is T/2 FLOP/B, so halving T halves it: each loaded value is reused 64 times instead of 128. The GEMM's total FLOPs (2MNK) do not change; only how often each byte is reused on chip.

lessons.title: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token

blocks.md: In your GPT, generating text means running the forward pass, sampling a token, appending it, and repeating. Serving systems split this into two phases (the paper behind vLLM, a widely used open-source serving engine, names them the *prompt phase* and the *autoregressive generation phase*; most engineers say **prefill** and **decode**).

blocks.title: A generation loop with a KV cache
blocks.code:
def generate(model, prompt_ids, n_new):
    cache = model.empty_kv_cache()
    # prefill: every prompt token in one pass
    logits = model(prompt_ids, cache)
    tok = argmax(logits[-1])
    out = [tok]
    for _ in range(n_new - 1):
        # decode: one new token per pass
        logits = model([tok], cache)
        tok = argmax(logits[-1])
        out.append(tok)
    return out

scenes.caption: The cache holds each layer's keys and values for tokens already processed (lesson 5 covers it in detail). It starts empty.
Prefill runs all 4 prompt tokens through the model in one pass. Every weight matrix multiplies a 4-row matrix, so each weight byte is reused 4 times.
The last position's logits give the first new token. This moment is the time to first token (TTFT).
Decode feeds only the newest token. The model still reads every weight, but uses each one for a single row: a matrix-vector product.
Each further step adds one token to the output and one entry per layer to the cache. Steps cannot run in parallel, since each needs the previous token.
After n_new tokens the loop returns. The time between consecutive tokens is the inter-token latency (ITL); its average over a request is the time per output token (TPOT).

blocks.md: How much work is one pass? Kaplan et al. (2020) count the forward-pass compute of a decoder Transformer with $N$ non-embedding parameters (every weight except the token and position embedding tables) as about $2N$ FLOPs per token: each parameter takes part in one multiply and one add. Attention adds work that grows with context length. In each of $n_{\text{layer}}$ layers a new token at context length $n_{\text{ctx}}$ takes a dot product with $n_{\text{ctx}}$ keys, then a weighted sum of $n_{\text{ctx}}$ values, both of width $d_{\text{attn}}$ (the width of the attention output, equal to the model width in these models): two multiply-and-add passes, so $4\,n_{\text{layer}}\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,d_{\text{attn}}$ FLOPs. The PaLM paper counts it the same way; Kaplan's table lists only the score product, $2\,n_{\text{layer}}\,n_{\text{ctx}}\,d_{\text{attn}}$, half of it.

blocks.tex: C_{\text{forward}} \approx 2N + 4\, n_{\text{layer}}\, n_{\text{ctx}}\, d_{\text{attn}}\quad\text{FLOPs per generated token}

blocks.md:
Worked example: **LLaMA-7B** (6.7B parameters, 32 layers, model width 4096, per the LLaMA paper; Llama 2 7B keeps this shape) in FP16 on one A100 80GB.

- Weights: $6.7\times10^9 \times 2$ bytes $= 13.4$ GB.
- Compute per token: about 2 FLOPs per parameter, $\approx 13.4$ GFLOP (Kaplan's $N$ excludes embeddings, so this slightly overcounts). At a 4096-token context the attention term is $4\times32\times4096\times4096 \approx 2.15$ GFLOP, about 16% more, so we leave it out of this first estimate.

That 16% holds only at moderate context. The attention term per token is $4\times32\times n_{\text{ctx}}\times4096$ FLOPs for LLaMA-7B, against $2N\approx13.4$ GFLOP for the weights:

- 4K tokens: 2.15 GFLOP, 16% of the weight term.
- 32K tokens: 17.2 GFLOP, 128%: attention now costs more than every weight matrix together.
- 128K tokens: 68.7 GFLOP, 513%.

LLaMA-7B was trained with 2K-token contexts and Llama 2 with 4K, so the long contexts are hypothetical for this shape, but newer models serve them.

blocks.title: LLaMA-7B FLOPs per token: weights vs attention

curves.label: attention: 4 x layers x ctx x 4096

scenes.caption: At the 4K context of the worked example, attention adds 2.15 GFLOP to 13.4: small enough to leave out of a first estimate.
The attention term grows linearly with context. The two lines cross near 26K tokens; beyond that, attention dominates the FLOPs of every new token.

blocks.md: In prefill, each of the $n$ prompt tokens attends to the tokens before it, so attention over the whole prompt grows with $n^2$: summing the per-token term over a 32K prompt gives about 281 TFLOP, against 439 TFLOP for the weight matmuls. Computed naively it would also write an $n\times n$ score matrix to HBM. FlashAttention computes attention in tiles that stay on chip, so long prompts cost FLOPs but not that extra memory traffic; the *FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4* course covers how.

blocks.prompt: Decoding one token for one user: is it limited by the 13.4 GFLOP of math, or by reading 13.4 GB of weights? Estimate the time for each on the A100.
blocks.reveal: Math: $13.4\times10^9 / 312\times10^{12} \approx 0.043$ ms. Memory: $13.4\times10^9 / 2.039\times10^{12} \approx 6.57$ ms. Memory wins by about 150x, so a single stream can produce at most about **152 tokens/s**, whatever the Tensor Cores can do.

blocks.caption: A lower bound for batch-1 decode; real systems add KV-cache reads, kernel launches and imperfect bandwidth use.

blocks.md: Prefill is different. A 1000-token prompt multiplies every weight by 1000 rows, about 13.4 TFLOP of work for the same 13.4 GB of weight reads. Its intensity is far above the ridge, so it is math-bound: ideally about 43 ms at peak, while reading the weights takes only 6.6 ms.

blocks.title: One request: compute-bound prefill, then memory-bound decode

scenes.caption: Idealised model (peak FLOP/s and peak bandwidth, no queueing or network): prefill of a 1000-token prompt is about 42.9 ms of math.
The first token appears when prefill ends: TTFT about 43 ms. Longer prompts mean longer TTFT.
Each decode step re-reads all 13.4 GB of weights, about 6.57 ms. That sets the inter-token latency and the streaming speed you see.

blocks.md: Prefill is math-bound (many tokens share each weight read). Decode is memory-bound (one token per weight read). Most GPU time in a long answer goes to decode, and the floor for each decode step is weight bytes divided by bandwidth.

Doubling peak TFLOP/s does almost nothing for batch-1 decode. What helps is moving fewer bytes per token (smaller or quantized weights: quantizing stores each weight in fewer bits, so 8-bit weights halve the bytes; the next lesson) or using each byte for more tokens (batching, lesson 6).

blocks.question: A 13B-parameter FP16 model runs on the same A100 at batch 1. Roughly what is the best-case decode speed?
options: About 78 tokens/s
About 152 tokens/s, the same as 7B
About 24,000 tokens/s
It depends only on the prompt length
blocks.explain: Weights are 26 GB; 26 GB / 2.039 TB/s is about 12.8 ms per token, or about 78 tokens/s. Decode time scales with bytes read, so twice the parameters means roughly half the speed.

blocks.question: Which change most reduces time to first token for a request with a very long prompt?
options: Faster HBM only
More math throughput (or splitting prefill across GPUs), since prefill is compute-bound
A larger decode batch
Lowering the number of output tokens
blocks.explain: TTFT is dominated by prefill (plus any queueing), and prefill of many tokens is compute-bound. Output length affects total latency, not TTFT.

lessons.title: Fewer bytes per weight: number formats and weight-only quantization

blocks.md:
The decode floor of the last lesson is a fraction: weight bytes over bandwidth. You cannot change the A100's 2,039 GB/s or LLaMA-7B's 6.7 billion parameters, but you can change how many bytes each parameter takes.

Tiny example: four weights 0.12, -0.50, 0.33, 0.07 cost 8 bytes in FP16. Instead store one shared FP16 **scale**, the largest magnitude over 7, here $0.50/7\approx0.0714$, and each weight as a 4-bit integer from -8 to 7: round 0.12/0.0714 and so on to get 2, -7, 5, 1. That is 2 bytes of integers plus 2 bytes of scale, 4 bytes in all. Multiplying back gives 0.143, -0.500, 0.357, 0.071: close, not exact.

That is **quantization**: storing values as small integers plus a scale. Rounding each value to the nearest integer step, as above, is called **round to nearest** (RTN). Bytes per parameter for the common formats:

- FP32: 4 bytes. BF16 or FP16: 2 bytes (both 16-bit floats; BF16 trades mantissa bits for FP32's exponent range).
- FP8 or INT8: 1 byte.
- INT4: 0.5 bytes, plus the scales. One FP16 scale per **group** of 128 weights adds $16/128 = 0.125$ bits, so 4.125 bits per weight.

The bit layouts of FP8 and FP4 belong to the *FP8 and FP4 training* course; here only the byte count matters.

blocks.caption: The same floor as lesson 3, with the bytes per weight made explicit. N = 6.7 billion for LLaMA-7B.

blocks.title: LLaMA-7B on one A100: weight size and batch-1 decode floor per format

scenes.caption: Weight memory in GB: 26.8, 13.4, 6.7 and 3.45. The INT4 bar includes the scales (4.125 bits per weight).
Decode floor in ms per token at 2,039 GB/s: 13.1, 6.57, 3.29 and 1.69. Each halving of bytes halves the floor.
The same floor as tokens per second for one user: about 76, 152, 304 and 590. Real kernels reach less (see the measured numbers below).

blocks.prompt: At batch 1, a decode step does about $2N$ FLOPs. On the roofline of lesson 2, where does the point for FP16, INT8 and INT4 weights sit?
blocks.reveal: Intensity is FLOPs over bytes. FLOPs stay $2N$; bytes fall from $2N$ to $N$ to about $0.52N$. So intensity goes from **1** to **2** to about **3.9** FLOP/B. The point slides right along the sloped, memory-bound part of the roof and its attainable FLOP/s rises in proportion, from about 2 to about 8 TFLOP/s. It is still far left of the ridge at 153: quantized decode is still memory-bound, just with fewer bytes.

blocks.md:
How can the matmul use 4-bit weights? In **weight-only quantization** the weights sit in HBM in low-bit form. The kernel loads the packed integers, multiplies them by their scale in registers (**dequantizes**) and does the math in 16-bit; activations stay 16-bit throughout. The write-up of gpt-fast, the PyTorch team's small reference implementation of LLM inference in plain PyTorch, says exactly this of its INT8 path: only the weights are quantized, and the computation itself is still done in BF16. Bytes fall, FLOPs do not, so it helps memory-bound decode and does almost nothing for compute-bound prefill.

The dequantize step must happen inside the matmul kernel. gpt-fast found INT8 weights without a fused kernel ran slower than FP16; the *Kernel fusion* course explains why steps left in separate kernels cost extra HBM traffic and launches.

To speed up prefill you must also quantize the activations, so the multiply itself runs in low precision. With INT8 weights and INT8 activations (W8A8), the A100's INT8 Tensor Cores are rated at 624 TOPS (tera integer operations per second) dense, twice the 312 TFLOP/s of FP16 (not the sparse FP16 624 of lesson 1). That raises the flat part of the roof, which is what a math-bound prefill needs.

blocks.title: Batch-1 decode ceiling for LLaMA-7B vs bits per weight

scenes.caption: Tokens per second is inversely proportional to bits per weight. Going from 16 to 8 bits gains 152 tokens/s; going from 8 to 4.125 gains another 286.
A chip with 3.35 TB/s lifts the whole curve by the bandwidth ratio. Quantization and faster memory multiply together.

blocks.md: Try it on CPU. The script below applies round to nearest to a random $4096\times4096$ matrix and to one real layer of Qwen2.5-0.5B (a 0.5-billion-parameter open model from Alibaba's Qwen team), as INT8 with one scale per row and as INT4 with one scale per 128 weights, and reports the error of $y = Wx$ relative to $\lVert y\rVert$. It stores the integers unpacked for clarity; the byte count assumes they are packed.

blocks.code:
import torch
torch.manual_seed(0)

def quantize(W, bits, group):
    # round to nearest, one FP16 scale per `group` weights of a row
    qmax = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1                  # 7 for int4, 127 for int8
    Wg = W.reshape(W.shape[0], -1, group)
    scale = (Wg.abs().amax(-1, keepdim=True) / qmax).half()
    q = torch.clamp(torch.round(Wg / scale.float()), -qmax - 1, qmax)
    return (q * scale.float()).reshape(W.shape), scale.numel()

def report(name, W):
    x = torch.randn(W.shape[1])
    y = W @ x
    for bits, group in [(8, W.shape[1]), (4, 128)]:
        Wq, n_scales = quantize(W, bits, group)
        nbytes = W.numel() * bits / 8 + n_scales * 2
        err = ((W @ x - Wq @ x).norm() / y.norm()).item()
        print(f"{name} int{bits} group {group}: "
              f"{8 * nbytes / W.numel():.3f} bits/weight, "
              f"{nbytes / (W.numel() * 2):.3f} of FP16 bytes, "
              f"error of Wx {err:.4f}")

report("random 4096x4096", torch.randn(4096, 4096) * 0.02)

from safetensors import safe_open    # a real layer, if the model is cached
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
path = hf_hub_download("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B", "model.safetensors")
with safe_open(path, "pt") as f:
    W = f.get_tensor("model.layers.0.mlp.down_proj.weight").float()
report(f"Qwen2.5-0.5B down_proj {tuple(W.shape)}", W)
blocks.caption: Round-to-nearest quantization of one matrix. Run with PyTorch 2.15 on CPU; the layer comes from the cached Qwen2.5-0.5B checkpoint.

blocks.md:
Output from the run:

```
random 4096x4096 int8 group 4096: 8.004 bits/weight, 0.500 of FP16 bytes, error of Wx 0.0089
random 4096x4096 int4 group 128: 4.125 bits/weight, 0.258 of FP16 bytes, error of Wx 0.1210
Qwen2.5-0.5B down_proj (896, 4864) int8 group 4864: 8.003 bits/weight, 0.500 of FP16 bytes, error of Wx 0.0119
Qwen2.5-0.5B down_proj (896, 4864) int4 group 128: 4.125 bits/weight, 0.258 of FP16 bytes, error of Wx 0.1342
```

INT8 with a scale per row costs half the bytes and moves $y$ by about 1%. INT4 with group 128 costs about a quarter of the bytes, but each layer's output moves by 12 to 13% on a random input. Whether the whole model still answers well has to be measured end to end; this per-layer error is what better methods attack.

Better methods, in one line each:

- [LLM.int8()](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07339): large models have a few **outlier feature** dimensions; it multiplies those in 16-bit and more than 99.9% of values in 8-bit.
- [GPTQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323): uses approximate second-order information to choose 3 or 4-bit weights that keep each layer's output close; a 175B model quantizes in about four GPU hours.
- [AWQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978): protecting about 1% of salient weight channels, found from activation magnitudes, cuts the error; it protects them by scaling, not by keeping them in higher precision.

The *Edge AI* course teaches the scale-and-zero-point quantization, per-channel scales and calibration these methods build on. Serving engines load such checkpoints directly:

blocks.code:
# Hugging Face: the method is read from the checkpoint's config.json
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("TheBloke/zephyr-7B-alpha-AWQ", device_map="auto")

# vLLM
from vllm import LLM
llm = LLM(model="TheBloke/Llama-2-7b-Chat-AWQ", quantization="auto_awq")
blocks.caption: Not run here (needs an NVIDIA GPU). From the Hugging Face quantization overview and vLLM's AutoAWQ page.

blocks.md: Published measurements show the effect. PyTorch's gpt-fast ran a 7B Llama at batch 1 on an A100-80GB (power-limited to 330 W): 107 tokens/s in 16-bit after compilation, 157.4 with INT8 weight-only quantization (one scale per row) and 202.1 with INT4 (GPTQ, groups of 32 weights). Faster each time, but not 2x and 4x: the floors at those sizes are about 304 and 487 tokens/s. The INT4 floor assumes 5 bits, not 4.5: each group of 32 stores a BF16 scale and a BF16 **zero point**, an offset that lets the 16 integer levels span the group's own minimum to maximum instead of a range centred on zero. That is $4 + 32/32 = 5$ bits per weight. Lesson 8 explains how to read that gap.

Quality loss depends on the model, the task and the method. gpt-fast saw no perceptible loss from INT8 weights but a measurable one at INT4, and Databricks warns that naive quantization can degrade quality substantially. Measure perplexity and a downstream task before shipping.
Decode time per token is about weight bytes over bandwidth, so halving bits per weight roughly halves it. Weight-only quantization cuts bytes, not FLOPs: it speeds decode, not prefill.

blocks.question: LLaMA-7B moves from FP16 to INT4 weight-only quantization on an A100. Roughly what happens to the time to first token for a 4,000-token prompt?
options: It drops about 4x, like the decode floor
Almost nothing: prefill needs about 53.6 TFLOP, about 172 ms of math, and weight reads (6.6 ms in FP16) were already hidden under it
It doubles, because dequantizing costs extra FLOPs
It drops 2x, because INT4 math is twice as fast
blocks.explain: Prefill of 4,000 tokens is $2\times6.7\times10^9\times4000\approx53.6$ TFLOP, about 172 ms at 312 TFLOP/s. Reading the weights took only 6.6 ms in FP16 and is overlapped with that math. Weight-only INT4 still computes in 16-bit, so the math is unchanged. Speeding up prefill needs low-precision compute (W8A8, FP8).

blocks.question: A capacity script estimates INT4 weight memory as parameters x 0.5 bytes. For LLaMA-7B quantized with one FP16 scale per 32 weights, what does it miss?
options: Nothing: scales are stored in host memory
The KV cache, which is part of the weights
INT4 is padded to 8 bits in HBM, so it is really 6.7 GB
The scales: 16/32 = 0.5 extra bits per weight, so 4.5 bits and about 3.77 GB, not 3.35 GB
blocks.explain: Each group of 32 weights carries a 16-bit scale, 0.5 extra bits per weight. That is 12.5% more bytes, and also a 12.5% slower decode floor. Smaller groups are more accurate and cost more. Storing a 16-bit zero point per group as well, as gpt-fast's INT4 does, adds another 0.5 bits: 5 bits, about 4.19 GB.

lessons.title: The KV cache: why memory grows with every token

blocks.md: In attention, the new token's query is compared against the **keys** of every earlier token, and the result mixes their **values**. Those keys and values depend only on earlier tokens, so they never change once computed. A naive loop recomputes them every step anyway.

blocks.prompt: A prompt has 4 tokens and we generate 4 more. Without a cache each step re-runs the whole sequence; with a cache each decode step processes only the newest token. How many token positions go through the model in each case?
blocks.reveal: Without a cache: $4 + 5 + 6 + 7 = 22$ positions. With a cache: 4 in prefill, then 1 per step for the 3 later steps, so **7**. The gap grows quadratically with length, which is why every serving system keeps a **KV cache**.

blocks.title: One layer's KV cache filling up during generation

scenes.caption: A 4-token prompt arrives. Nothing is cached yet.
Prefill computes keys and values for all 4 positions at once and stores them. This happens in every layer, for every KV head (each head keeps its own keys and values).
Decode step 1: the new token 'the' computes only its own k5 and v5. Its query attends over k1 to k5, which are read from HBM.
Each later step appends one entry. Compute per step stays small, but the bytes read per step grow with the context.

blocks.md: Size per token: every layer stores one key vector and one value vector per KV head. For standard multi-head attention every head has its own keys and values, so the KV heads are simply the heads, and together they span the model width: LLaMA-7B has 32 heads of width $d_{\text{head}} = 128$, and $32\times128 = 4096$.

blocks.tex: \text{KV bytes per token} = 2 \times n_{\text{layer}} \times n_{\text{kv heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes per value}
blocks.caption: Two vectors (a key and a value), in every layer, for every key-value head, each d_head numbers long, at the number's size in bytes.

blocks.md: LLaMA-7B in FP16: $2 \times 32 \times 4096 \times 2 = 524,288$ bytes, exactly 512 KiB per token. A kibibyte is $2^{10} = 1{,}024$ bytes, the power-of-two cousin of the 1,000-byte kilobyte, and $524{,}288 / 1{,}024 = 512$. A full 4096-token context therefore needs $4096 \times 512$ KiB = 2 GiB per sequence; a gibibyte is $2^{30}$ bytes, about 1.074 GB, so 2 GiB is about 2.15 GB. The vLLM paper does the same sum for OPT-13B, Meta's 13-billion-parameter Open Pre-trained Transformer: 800 KB per token and up to 1.6 GB per 2048-token request.

blocks.title: Where an 80 GB A100 goes when serving LLaMA-7B

scenes.caption: Weights take 13.4 GB. One full-length sequence's KV cache is 2.15 GB (2 GiB).
Simplified: ignoring activations and framework overhead, 66.6 GB is left for KV cache, which holds about 31 full 4096-token sequences (last bar is a count, not GB).

Grouped-query attention lets several query heads share one key and value head. With 8 KV heads instead of 32 (GQA-8), KV per token drops 4x to 128 KiB, so about 124 sequences fit. Hypothetical for this 7B shape.

blocks.md:
Two consequences follow. First, the number of requests you can decode at once is usually capped by KV memory, not compute. Second, each decode step must read the cache of every sequence in the batch, so long contexts add HBM traffic on top of the weights.

This is why Llama 2's 34B and 70B models adopted **grouped-query attention** (GQA): sharing key and value heads across query heads shrinks the cache. GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) was designed to keep quality close to multi-head attention while cutting this memory bandwidth and capacity.

Reserving the maximum length for every request wastes most of the cache. vLLM's profiling found only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory held actual token states in earlier systems, due to reserved slots and fragmentation. PagedAttention fixes this by allocating the cache in small fixed-size blocks, like OS pages.
KV cache size = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dim x bytes, per token, per sequence. It grows linearly with context and with batch size, and it is usually what limits how many users one GPU can serve.

blocks.question: A team switches a model from 32 KV heads to 8 (GQA), keeping everything else. What changes most directly?
options: KV cache per token shrinks 4x, so more or longer sequences fit and decode reads fewer cache bytes
Weights shrink by 4x
Prefill FLOPs drop 4x
Context length must be cut by 4x
blocks.explain: Only the key and value projections shrink, which are a small part of the weights. The cache stores 8 instead of 32 heads per layer, a 4x reduction in KV memory and KV traffic.

blocks.question: A server runs LLaMA-7B in FP16 on an 80 GB A100 with 2048-token contexts. Ignoring overheads, roughly how many full sequences fit in the KV space?
options: About 31
About 2,048
About 62
Unlimited, KV lives in host memory
blocks.explain: Each sequence needs 2048 x 512 KiB = 1 GiB (about 1.07 GB). 66.6 GB / 1.07 GB is about 62. Halving the context doubles how many fit.

lessons.title: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users

blocks.md: Batch-1 decode used under 1% of the A100's math. The fix comes straight from the roofline: if $B$ sequences decode together, each weight read from HBM is used for $B$ tokens, so arithmetic intensity rises to roughly $B$ FLOP/B while the weight bytes stay the same: $B$ tokens need $2N$ FLOPs each, $2NB$ in all, against $2N$ bytes of FP16 weights, and $2NB / 2N = B$.

blocks.caption: Step time is the larger of math time (2N FLOPs per token times B tokens, over peak) and memory time (2N weight bytes plus B caches of n_ctx tokens at s_kv = 512 KiB each, over bandwidth). Throughput is B over step time. Attention FLOPs, overheads ignored.

blocks.prompt: Ignore the KV cache for a moment (n_ctx = 0). At batch 64, how long is one decode step for LLaMA-7B on an A100, and how many tokens/s does the GPU produce?
blocks.reveal: Math: $64 \times 0.0429$ ms $= 2.75$ ms. Memory: still 6.57 ms for the weights. The step stays **6.57 ms**, now producing 64 tokens: about **9,739 tokens/s**. Batching up to the ridge (about 153) is nearly free for each user.

blocks.title: Decode throughput vs batch size for LLaMA-7B on one A100

scenes.caption: Weights only: throughput rises linearly until batch about 153, then flattens at the math roof, about 23,284 tokens/s. That 153 holds only at zero context; KV-cache reads bend the curve far earlier, as the next scene shows.
Add KV reads at 1024 tokens of context: each step reads 13.4 GB of weights plus 64 x 1024 x 512 KiB (34.4 GB) of cache: 23.4 ms, about 2,732 tokens/s. Cache traffic, not math, now limits the curve.
At 4096 tokens of context the cache fills HBM at about 31 sequences, giving about 790 tokens/s with 39 ms steps.
Short contexts let you batch far more before memory runs out. Drag the slider: both throughput and the memory wall move with context length.

blocks.md:
Batching trades latency for throughput. In this model at 1024 tokens of context, batch 1 reads 13.4 GB of weights plus 0.54 GB of cache per step, 6.84 ms, so one user gets about 146 tokens/s; batch 64 takes 23.4 ms per step, so each user gets about 43 tokens/s but the GPU as a whole about 64 / 23.4 ms, or 2,732. Serving teams pick a batch size (or a latency target) on this curve.

The metrics: **TTFT** (time to first token), which includes queueing and prefill; **ITL**, each gap between output tokens, and **TPOT**, their average over a request; and **tokens per second** across all requests.

Requests arrive at different times and stop at different lengths. With **static batching** a batch runs until its longest request finishes; short requests leave their slot idle and new arrivals wait. Orca, a research serving system presented at OSDI 2022 (the USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation), introduced **iteration-level scheduling**: after every decode step finished requests leave and waiting ones join. vLLM and most modern servers do this, usually called **continuous batching**.

blocks.title: Static vs continuous batching with 3 batch slots

scenes.caption: Static: A, B and C start together; the batch ends only when A finishes at step 8. Slots 2 and 3 sit idle once B and C finish.
D and E then run as a second batch. All 5 requests finish at step 12; the slots do useful work 61% of the time.
Continuous: D takes slot 2 the moment B finishes, and E takes slot 3 after C. Everything finishes by step 8, with 92% slot use. Simplified: prefill of joiners is ignored.

blocks.md:
Continuous batching creates a new problem. A request that joins must first run its prefill, and in a simple engine that prefill runs in the same step as everyone else's decode. With 32 users decoding LLaMA-7B, a step is about 6.6 ms (weight reads; KV reads ignored here). If a 2,000-token prompt joins, that step must also do $2\times6.7\times10^9\times2000\approx26.8$ TFLOP, about 86 ms at peak: twice the 1,000-token prefill of lesson 3. The step takes about 87 ms, and all 32 users wait about 13 times longer than usual for their next token.

Two fixes exist: **chunked prefill** splits a long prompt across several steps, and **prefill/decode disaggregation** runs the two phases on different GPUs. The *Disaggregated prefill and decode* course compares them.

blocks.title: A joining prefill stalls every decoding user

scenes.caption: Steady state, batch 32: each decode step is about 6.6 ms, and user 1 gets a token at the end of each step.

A 2,000-token prompt joins. Its prefill (about 86 ms of math) shares the step with 32 decodes, so the step ends near 107 ms. User 1 waits 87 ms for the next token instead of 6.6 ms. Idealised: peak FLOP/s, no overheads.

blocks.md: Decode is memory-bound, so throughput comes from making every weight read serve many tokens. Batch size is capped by KV-cache memory, and continuous batching keeps that batch full as requests come and go.

Bigger batches are not free for users: once the step leaves the flat region (math roof, or growing KV reads), every sequence's inter-token latency rises. A throughput number without a latency number hides this.

blocks.question: A service at batch 8 is far below the ridge, and its GPU has plenty of free HBM. Users complain throughput per GPU is low but latency is fine. What should the team try first?
options: Buy a GPU with more TFLOP/s
Lower the batch size to 1
Disable the KV cache to save memory
Raise the batch size (or admit more concurrent requests): each step costs about the same, so throughput rises almost linearly
blocks.explain: Below the ridge each step is dominated by reading the weights, so adding sequences adds tokens at nearly no extra time per step until KV reads or math catch up. More FLOP/s does not help a memory-bound step.

blocks.question: Why does continuous batching improve throughput over static batching?
options: Finished requests free their slot right away and waiting requests join at the next step, so fewer slots sit idle
It makes each decode step faster
It removes the need for a KV cache
It runs prefill and decode on different GPUs
blocks.explain: The step time is unchanged; what changes is how full the batch is. Iteration-level scheduling refills slots every iteration instead of waiting for the longest request.

lessons.title: When one GPU is not enough: tensor parallelism and the decode floor

blocks.md: Every example so far fits on one GPU. Llama 2 70B does not: it has 80 layers of width 8192 and about 70 billion parameters, so its FP16 weights are about 140 GB, and an A100 holds 80 GB. Even INT8 weights (70 GB) would leave about 10 GB for the KV cache. The model must be split across GPUs, and how you split it decides the latency.

**Tensor parallelism** (TP), as in Megatron-LM (NVIDIA's 2019 paper and library for splitting Transformer layers across GPUs), splits every layer across $T$ GPUs. Tiny example with $T = 2$ and an MLP $Y = \text{GeLU}(XA)$, $Z = YB$:

1. Split $A$ by columns: GPU 0 holds $A_1$, GPU 1 holds $A_2$. Each computes its half of $Y$ and applies GeLU on its own, because GeLU works element by element.
2. Split $B$ by rows to match. Each GPU multiplies its half of $Y$ by its half of $B$, giving a full-size **partial sum** of $Z$.
3. An **all-reduce** adds the partial sums: every GPU contributes a tensor of the same shape and every GPU receives the elementwise sum.

Attention splits the same way, by heads for Q, K and V and by rows for the output projection. Megatron-LM's paper notes the whole layer then needs only two all-reduces in the forward pass, one after attention and one after the MLP.

scenes.caption: Both GPUs start with the same input X. Each holds half of every weight matrix, so each reads half the bytes per token.
Column split: each GPU computes half of the hidden units and applies GeLU without talking to the other.
Row split: each GPU multiplies its half of Y by its rows of B. Each result is full size but only a partial sum.
One all-reduce adds the partial sums so both GPUs hold Z. Per layer: one of these after attention, one after the MLP.

blocks.md: For decode, the win is bandwidth. With $T$ GPUs each one reads only $1/T$ of the weight bytes per token, in parallel, so the bandwidth floor divides by $T$. The cost is $2\,n_{\text{layer}}$ all-reduces per token, and at batch 1 each one moves very little data: one activation vector of 8,192 FP16 values, 16 KiB. Over NVLink, NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link (600 GB/s per A100, both directions counted), that is tens of nanoseconds of transfer, so each all-reduce costs mostly a fixed **latency** that does not shrink as $T$ grows. Google's scaling book says the same: collectives on activations are often bound by the latency term, especially at small batch sizes.

blocks.caption: A simplified model for batch-1 decode. It ignores KV reads, kernel launches and other per-step costs, which also do not shrink with T.

blocks.prompt: Llama 2 70B in FP16 on A100s. Assume each all-reduce costs 20 microseconds (an assumption for this model, not a measured number). What is the per-token time at T = 2, 4 and 8, and how much faster is 8 than 4?
blocks.reveal: Floor: $140\ \text{GB} / (T\times2.039\ \text{TB/s})$ = **34.3, 17.2 and 8.6 ms**. Communication: $2\times80 = 160$ all-reduces x 20 us = **3.2 ms** at every $T$. Totals: 37.5, 20.4 and 11.8 ms. Going from 4 to 8 GPUs gives 1.73x, not 2x, and the gap widens as $T$ grows, because the fixed term becomes a bigger share.

blocks.title: Llama 2 70B batch-1 decode time vs tensor-parallel degree

scenes.caption: Bandwidth alone: the floor halves each time T doubles. The model needs T of at least 2 to fit at all (140 GB over 80 GB per GPU).
Add 160 all-reduces of 20 us each: a flat 3.2 ms that no number of GPUs removes. At T = 8 it is already over a quarter of the step.
With 50 us per all-reduce, 8 GPUs give 16.6 ms against 25.2 ms for 4: only 1.5x. Drag the slider to see how the payoff of more GPUs depends on it.

blocks.md: Measurements agree in shape. Databricks reports that for inference, unlike training, more GPUs give strongly diminishing latency returns: for Llama2-70B, "going from 4x to 8x GPUs only decreases latency by 0.7x at small batch sizes", and for MPT-7B (MosaicML's 7-billion-parameter model) at batch 1, going from 2 to 4 GPUs cut token latency by only about 12%. At batch 16 the same move to 4 GPUs cut MPT-7B latency by 33%, since a larger batch gives each GPU more work per step to set against the fixed costs.

Two other ways to split, and what they do for latency:

- **Pipeline parallelism** (PP) gives each GPU a contiguous range of layers. The model fits, but one token still walks through every stage in order, so single-request latency is no better than one very large GPU. It helps throughput when many requests fill the pipeline.
- **Data parallelism** (DP) runs full copies of the model, each serving its own requests. Throughput scales with copies; latency per request does not change, and each copy must fit.

vLLM's guidance follows: use tensor parallelism inside one node, add pipeline parallelism across nodes, and prefer pipeline parallelism on GPUs without NVLink.

blocks.code:
from vllm import LLM
llm = LLM("facebook/opt-13b", tensor_parallel_size=4)
print(llm.generate("San Francisco is a"))

# the same from the command line, 4 GPUs of tensor parallelism
# vllm serve facebook/opt-13b --tensor-parallel-size 4
# 8 GPUs: 4-way tensor parallel x 2 pipeline stages
# vllm serve gpt2 --tensor-parallel-size 4 --pipeline-parallel-size 2
blocks.caption: Not run here (needs several NVIDIA GPUs). From vLLM's parallelism and scaling docs.

blocks.md:
**Mixture of experts** (MoE) bends the bytes-per-token rule. Mixtral 8x7B has 8 expert MLPs per layer and a router that picks 2 of them for each token: about 47B parameters stored, but only about 13B used per token. In FP16 that is 94 GB to hold, so two A100s at least, yet a batch-1 decode step reads only about 26 GB, about 12.8 ms at one A100's bandwidth instead of 46 ms for a dense 47B model.

At larger batch the saving fades. Different tokens pick different experts, and in a simplified model where each token picks 2 of 8 uniformly at random, an expert is skipped by one token with probability 0.75 and by all 16 tokens of a batch with $0.75^{16}\approx1\%$. So at batch 16 nearly every expert is read in every step, and decode reads almost all 94 GB.

blocks.title: Mixtral 8x7B in FP16: bytes held vs bytes read per decode step

scenes.caption: All 47B parameters must sit in memory: 94 GB. A single token reads the shared layers plus 2 of 8 experts per layer, about 26 GB.

Simplified, uniform random routing: at batch 4 an expert is untouched with probability 0.75 to the 4th, 32%, so about 65 GB is read; at batch 16 about 93 GB. The MoE byte saving is a small-batch effect.

blocks.md: Google's scaling book makes the same point in roofline terms: memory grows with the number of experts $E$ while FLOPs grow only with the number chosen $k$, so an MoE needs about $E/k$ times the batch of a dense model before decode stops being memory-bound. How experts are spread over GPUs (expert parallelism and its all-to-all traffic) is in the last lesson of the *Fine-grained MoE* course; the training-side splits are in the *Megatron-Core performance* course.

More GPUs do not automatically mean lower latency. Pipeline and data parallelism add capacity and throughput but leave single-request latency where it was, and tensor parallelism hits a floor set by per-layer communication latency.

Tensor parallelism divides each token's weight bytes across T GPUs, so the decode floor falls about as 1/T, but every layer adds two all-reduces whose latency does not shrink. MoE models read only the active experts at batch 1, yet must hold all of them.

blocks.question: A team serving a 70B model at batch 1 moves from 4 to 8 tensor-parallel GPUs and sees per-token latency fall only about 25%. What is the most likely reason?
options: The weights no longer fit in memory
Pipeline bubbles appear when T exceeds 4
Each GPU's share of weight reads halved, but the fixed per-layer all-reduce latency and other per-step costs did not, so they now dominate
NVLink bandwidth is saturated by the 16 KiB activations
blocks.explain: The bandwidth term halves with T, but 160 all-reduces per token cost roughly the same at any T, as do kernel launches. Moving 16 KiB over 600 GB/s takes tens of nanoseconds, so bandwidth is not the limit; latency is.

blocks.question: Which way of using more GPUs lowers the latency of a single decoding request?
options: Tensor parallelism, because each GPU reads only a slice of every layer's weights for the same token
Data parallelism, because there are more copies of the model
Pipeline parallelism, because the layers run on different GPUs
None of them can, since decode is memory-bound
blocks.explain: Only tensor parallelism splits the work of one token across GPUs at the same moment, adding their bandwidth together. Data parallelism serves more requests; pipeline parallelism makes one token visit the stages one after another.

lessons.title: Measure it: tokens per second, MBU and MFU

blocks.md:
Every number in this course so far is a prediction from bytes and FLOPs. Before trusting one, or choosing which lever to pull, you check it on hardware. Two ratios say how close a measurement came to the limits:

- **Model Bandwidth Utilization** (MBU), as Databricks defines it: achieved memory bandwidth over peak, where achieved bandwidth is (weight bytes + KV-cache bytes) divided by the time per output token.
- **Model FLOPs Utilization** (MFU), from the PaLM paper: observed throughput relative to the throughput the hardware would reach at peak FLOP/s.

Decode at small batch is memory-bound, so MBU is its yardstick; prefill and large batches are math-bound, so MFU is theirs. For example, gpt-fast's compiled 107 tokens/s (next block) is $107\times13.4$ GFLOP, about 1.4 TFLOP/s: an MFU under 0.5%, while its MBU is about 70%.

blocks.tex: \text{MBU} = \frac{(\text{weight bytes} + \text{KV bytes}) / t_{\text{token}}}{\text{peak bandwidth}},\qquad \text{MFU} = \frac{\text{tokens/s}\times\text{FLOPs per token}}{\text{peak FLOP/s}}
blocks.caption: MBU of 100% means each decode step takes exactly the floor of lesson 3. FLOPs per token is about 2N, plus attention at long context.

blocks.md:
A published worked example: PyTorch's gpt-fast team ran a 7B Llama at batch 1 on an A100-80GB, power-limited to 330 W. Their first, plain PyTorch version produced **25.5 tokens/s**, 39 ms per token against a floor of 6.57 ms: about 17% of the floor. Their profile showed the GPU mostly idle: the CPU, running Python, could not issue kernels as fast as the GPU finished them. At batch 1 every kernel is a tiny matrix-vector product, so launch cost, not HBM, sets the pace.

Compiling the decode step (`torch.compile` with CUDA graphs and a statically allocated KV cache) brought it to **107 tokens/s**, which the post computes as **72% MBU**; it notes that even a plain memory copy struggles to pass 85%. The *CPU and GPU co-scheduling* course explains CUDA graphs, and the *Kernel fusion* course explains what `torch.compile` fuses.

blocks.title: Predicted floor vs measured time per token, 7B Llama, A100, batch 1

scenes.caption: Plain eager PyTorch: 39.2 ms per token against a 6.57 ms floor. The gap is CPU launch overhead, not bandwidth.
Compiled: 9.35 ms (107 tokens/s), within about 1.4x of the floor. Now the weight bytes really are the limit.

Quantized: INT8 6.35 ms against a 3.29 ms floor, INT4 (5 bits with a scale and zero point per 32) 4.95 ms against 2.05 ms. Fewer bytes still help, but fixed per-step costs and dequantize work are a growing share.

blocks.md: Measuring it yourself takes care, because GPU work is asynchronous: a CUDA call returns as soon as the kernel is queued. The timer must wait with `torch.cuda.synchronize()` before reading the clock, the first calls (memory allocation, kernel selection, compilation) must be excluded as warm-up, and prefill must be timed separately from decode. The script below does all three and works on either device. Without an NVIDIA GPU it falls back to CPU, uses 2 threads, and measures a memory copy to stand in for peak bandwidth.

blocks.title: Timing prefill and decode, then computing MBU
blocks.code:
import time, torch
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
cuda = torch.cuda.is_available()
dev, dt = ("cuda", torch.bfloat16) if cuda else ("cpu", torch.float32)
sync = torch.cuda.synchronize if cuda else (lambda: None)
m = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B", dtype=dt).to(dev).eval()
n = sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
w_bytes = n * torch.finfo(dt).bits // 8
if cuda: roof = 2.039e12               # A100 80GB SXM datasheet
else:                                  # CPU: 2 threads, best copy bandwidth
    torch.set_num_threads(2); a = torch.empty(2**28, dtype=torch.uint8); ts = []
    for _ in range(5): t = time.perf_counter(); a.clone(); ts.append(time.perf_counter() - t)
    roof = 2 * a.numel() / min(ts)

@torch.no_grad()
def run(batch, prompt=256, steps=32):
    ids = torch.randint(0, 1000, (batch, prompt), device=dev)
    sync(); t0 = time.perf_counter()
    out = m(ids, use_cache=True)  # prefill
    sync(); t1 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(steps):  # decode
        tok = out.logits[:, -1:].argmax(-1)
        out = m(tok, past_key_values=out.past_key_values, use_cache=True)
    sync(); itl = (time.perf_counter() - t1) / steps
    return t1 - t0, itl

print(f"{dev}: {w_bytes/1e9:.2f} GB weights, roof {roof/1e9:.0f} GB/s, "
      f"floor {w_bytes/roof*1e3:.1f} ms/step")
run(1, steps=4)  # warm-up
for b in (1, 8):
    ttft, itl = run(b)
    print(f"batch {b}: TTFT {ttft*1e3:.0f} ms, ITL {itl*1e3:.1f} ms, {b/itl:.0f} tok/s, "
          f"MBU {w_bytes/itl/roof:.0%}, {2*n*b/itl/1e9:.0f} GFLOP/s")

scenes.caption: Pick the device. On a GPU the model runs in BF16 and the roof is the A100 datasheet's 2,039 GB/s; on CPU it runs in FP32.
Weight bytes: parameter count times bytes per value. Qwen2.5-0.5B has about 495M parameters; tied embeddings are counted once.
CPU only: the best of five 256 MiB copies (read plus write) is the stand-in roof, since no datasheet peak applies here.
synchronize, then start the clock: prefill of a 256-token prompt. Its time is the TTFT.

Decode loop: feed one token per sequence with the cache, 32 steps, then synchronize again and divide by the steps to get ITL. Newer transformers releases warn that past_key_values is being renamed; it still works.
One short warm-up run is thrown away, then batch 1 and batch 8 are measured.
scenes.output: cpu: 1.98 GB weights, roof 177 GB/s, floor 11.2 ms/step

scenes.caption: MBU here counts weight bytes only: the cache at 272 tokens is about 6.7 MB per sequence, negligible next to 1.98 GB.
scenes.output:
batch 1: TTFT 461 ms, ITL 27.0 ms, 37 tok/s, MBU 41%, 37 GFLOP/s
batch 8: TTFT 1495 ms, ITL 51.1 ms, 157 tok/s, MBU 22%, 155 GFLOP/s

blocks.md:
The full output of one run on an Apple M5 Pro CPU (2 threads, FP32, PyTorch 2.15.0, transformers 5.24.0). The GPU branch is not run here: this machine has no NVIDIA GPU.

```
cpu: 1.98 GB weights, roof 177 GB/s, floor 11.2 ms/step
batch 1: TTFT 461 ms, ITL 27.0 ms, 37 tok/s, MBU 41%, 37 GFLOP/s
batch 8: TTFT 1495 ms, ITL 51.1 ms, 157 tok/s, MBU 22%, 155 GFLOP/s
```

Read it with the course's model. At batch 1 the step takes 27 ms against an 11.2 ms floor, 41% MBU. At batch 8 the step takes only 1.9x longer for 8x the tokens, so throughput rises 4x, but MBU falls to 22%: at about 155 GFLOP/s, two CPU cores are probably near their math limit (this run did not measure their peak). The ridge of two CPU cores sits at a far lower batch than a GPU's. TTFT for the same prompt was 293 ms in another run, so repeat runs before trusting one.

Serving engines measure the same quantities under real load. vLLM ships a load generator, [`vllm bench serve`](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/cli/bench/serve.html), that reports percentiles of TTFT, ITL and TPOT; NVIDIA's NIM benchmarking guide defines the same metrics. The *LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management* course shows how the scheduler shapes them, and the *Tail latency* course how to read percentiles under load.

Published MBU numbers give a sense of what is achievable: Databricks measured about 60% MBU at batch 1 on 2 H100-80GB GPUs (the A100's successor) and 55% on 4 A100-40GB GPUs with TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA's inference engine), and found MBU falls as batch size grows, because larger batches move the step toward the math roof, where MFU becomes the number to watch.

Common timing mistakes: reading the clock without `torch.cuda.synchronize()` (you time the launch, not the work); including the first call (allocation and compilation); comparing tokens/s across different prompt lengths, output lengths or batch sizes; forgetting power and clock limits (gpt-fast's A100 was capped at 330 W). The *Microbenchmarking pitfalls* course covers the general rules.

Compare every measurement with its floor. MBU near 70 to 80% at small batch means the bytes are the limit, so cut bytes (quantize) or add bandwidth (tensor parallelism). MBU far lower means overhead: launches, Python, unfused kernels.

blocks.question: Batch-1 decode of a 7B FP16 model on an A100 measures 35% MBU. Which pair of causes is most likely?
options: The KV cache is too small, and the prompt is too short
Tensor Cores are too slow, and the clock is too high
Per-kernel launch overhead from eager Python code, and elementwise work not fused into the matmul kernels
Too many warps per SM, and too much L2 cache
blocks.explain: At batch 1 each kernel is tiny, so the time between kernels (Python, launches) is a large share of each step; gpt-fast went from about 17% to about 70% of the 6.57 ms floor by removing it (the post reports 72% MBU using a rounder 2 TB/s). Unfused extra kernels add reads and launches too. Math speed is irrelevant to a memory-bound step.

blocks.question: A benchmark times a decode step of a 7B FP16 model on an A100 with time.perf_counter() around model(x), without torch.cuda.synchronize(), and reports 0.2 ms per step. What does this tell you?
options: The model is running at 30x the bandwidth floor thanks to the L2 cache
The timer measured how long it took to queue the kernels, not run them: 0.2 ms is far below the 6.57 ms floor, so the number is impossible
Decode is math-bound at batch 1
The measurement is right, because perf_counter waits for the GPU
blocks.explain: 13.4 GB of weights cannot be read in 0.2 ms at 2.039 TB/s. CUDA launches are asynchronous, so without synchronize the clock stops while the GPU is still working. A result below the physical floor is a measurement bug.
